idiom_name: operator+ / operator* overloads returning the value type (Money operator+(const Money&, const Money&))
implementation_notes: C++ gives the arithmetic syntax directly: implement the binary operation as a member or hidden-friend operator+ that returns by value, defined in terms of operator+= on the canonical representation - cppreference's canonical form takes the left operand by value, reuses the compound assignment and returns the result, so the temporary is moved rather than copied. What replaces the classic structure is the language's operator overload mechanism plus the standard library's closed types (std::complex, std::chrono::duration, std::string), which show the intended shape and laws. Operators remain the right choice when combinations appear in expressions (a + b + c) or when the type imitates an arithmetic concept; for one-off combinations, or when the operation is not genuinely additive, a named member or free function reads better and keeps the metaphor honest. Keep the type immutable - const member operations, no mutating operand - so a + b + c cannot alias.
pitfalls: A closed signature that mutates shared state: implementing operator+ to modify and return the left operand breaks the value semantics the pattern assumes; return a new value and keep the mutating form to operator+=.
Returning a reference or a proxy from a combining operator is a lifetime trap - operator+ must return the value type by value, not a reference to a temporary or to a member.
Implicit converting constructors make closure lie: if Money can be built from an integer, money + 3 compiles and silently mixes units; mark such constructors explicit.
Signed overflow is undefined behaviour and each operator allocates a temporary, neither of which the arithmetic syntax reveals at a call site.
